segments.text: A Continuous-Time Causal Graph Learning Framework for Predicting and Mitigating Cascading Failures in Global Supply Chains Abstract- Global supply chains face increasing exposure to rapidly propagating disruptions triggered by geopolitical conflicts, climate-related shocks, and operational instabilities. Existing predictive approaches, including recent causal graph neural networks, remain limited by static causal structures, discrete-time reasoning, and post-hoc counterfactual analysis. These constraints reduce their ability to anticipate high-velocity cascade effects and to recommend proactive, cost-effective interventions. This work introduces CT-SCaLE, a novel Continuous-Time Structural Causal Learning Engine that unifies Neural ODE-based temporal dynamics, end-to-end differentiable causal structure learning, and counterfactual contrastive representation learning into a single predictive and decision-support architecture. CT-SCaLE learns both the evolving causal topology and the temporal propagation dynamics of disruptions, allowing the model to capture time-varying influences, multi-tier propagation patterns, and realistic feedback loops that traditional DAG-based causal GNNs cannot represent. Evaluations on SupplyGraph and Time-Series Risk datasets show that CT-SCaLE improves disruption prediction accuracy by up to 14.7%, increases early-warning lead time by 22%, and reduces simulated cascade size under optimized interventions by 31.4%, significantly outperforming advanced baselines. A central novelty is a built-in intervention planner based on models that uses multi-step counterfactual simulations to discover the minimum-cost actions that can mitigate or steer cascading failures. This addresses a crucial unmet need, predicting not just disruptions, but actionable causal explanations and mitigations. By incorporating prediction, explanation and intervention optimization in a continuous time framework, CT-SCaLE opens a new frontiers for supply chain analytics driving more resilient and adaptive global operations. Keywords-Causal Graph Neural Networks, Supply Chain Resilience, Neural ODEs, Causal Discovery, Counterfactual Learning, Cascading Failures, Intervention Optimization, Graph Machine Learning, Risk Prediction, Continuous-Time Modeling I Introduction Global supply chains have become complex and highly-linked, multi-level networked systems with localized disruptions cascading to system levels. The recent past has demonstrated that cascading failures are no longer rare, slow-moving outliers but high-velocity events grounded in geopolitics, extreme climate and infectious disease as well as infrastructural fault lines. Trade barriers, port closures, energy scarcity and regional conflicts now spread across borders within days or even hours rather than the previous months, quickly overpowering conventional risk cushions and recovery systems [1], [2]. Empirical works on the flow of global shipping, commodity trade, and supply chains of critical materials show how disturbances tend to trigger non-linear ripple effects whereby losses propagate well beyond the directly disrupted nodes [3][4][5]. Although organizations are paying more attention to making resilience more resilient, they tend toward a reactive rather proactive response. It waits till the disruption occurs before stopping the propagation of

This increasing disparity between rate of disruption and latency to a decision underscores the importance of predictive models that can foresee cascading failures before they happen and direct interventions in time. There is previous work that used machine learning and network analysis to predict supply chain risks, utilizing graph representations to capture inter-firm relationships and disruption spillover [8][9][10]. However, the vast majority of graph machine learning methods remain essentially correlation-based [11][12], learning statistical relationships rather than causal dependencies in failure propagation. Recently, the advanced causal graph neural networks employ a static directed acyclic graphs and implicitly assume that the causal effects are time-invariant and acyclic [17], [18]. There are some obvious flaws with this kind of assumption that do not correspond to the reality of supply chains: 1) asset strength scores change over time in real-world networks, as do loop/circuit counts; 2) sources of disruption appear and disappear when looking at the graph locally changes in response to human activity. Discretetime models increase unresponsiveness still more by binning events into coarse time bins, which may miss early cascades or see late ones [11][12]. In addition, counterfactual reasoning in previous models tends to be used post factum to rationalize predictions as opposed to being embedded into an optimization approach that considers actively identifying and evaluating prevention strategies under cost and timing constraints [15][16]. Consequently, existing approaches fall short in providing the real-time decision-driven approach for addressing cascading failures. To overcome these shortcomings, in this paper we present CT-SCaLE (Continuous-Time SCaLing Engine), for cascading failure prediction and mitigation in global supply chains. In contrast to prior methods, CT-SCaLE learns simultaneously the changing topology of causal supply chain networks and the continuous-time evolution dynamics of shock spreading. The proposed framework uses Neural Ordinary Differential Equations to represent high-resolution temporal change and design time varying causal influence, delayed effects and feedback-based escalation. The parsing of causal structure is then trained within the end-to-end pipeline, and can therefore adapt its causal graph as network conditions evolve. Crucially, CT-SCaLE is intervention-aware: it natively includes counterfactual reasoning in the learning and decision cascade, allowing for simulation and evaluation of pro-active mitigation measures over retrospective justifications. By integrating prediction, causality, and intervention planning in the presence of disturbances into a continuous-time framework, CT-SCaLE is positioned to satisfy the needs common to contemporary supply chains that are susceptible to disruptions. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: ●​ Continuous-time causality topological learning: To this end, we have devised a causal learning mechanism which we show is able to learn time-varying influence strengths and feedback loops beyond the static DAG representations. ●​ Joint cascade prediction and intervention modeling: Our CT-SCaLE unifies the above disruption forecasting along with multi-step intervention simulation in a single differentiable framework.
segments.label: human

segments.text: ●​ Counterfactual contrastive representation learning: Generates representations that are explicitly sensitive to the outcomes of interventions, and makes the model more robust to hypothetical conditions. ●​ Cost-Conscious Cascading Failure Mitigation: An in-network intervention planner which recognizes minimum-cost interventions to suppress or redirect disruption cascades before they spread at a large scale. Taken together, these contributions move supply-chain analytics from passive risk prediction to control of cascading processes in continuous time driven by causes, thereby filling a crucial gap in current resilience methodologies. The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 offers a detailed review on literature works concerning cascading failures, causal graph learning and supply chain resilience. The problem is formulated in Section 3 by introducing the continuous-time supply chain graph, dynamic causal structure and intervention framework. We present our proposed CT-SCaLE architecture in Section 4, which describes the continuous-time causal dynamics that parameters are learned against, the differentiable structure learning module, counterfactual contrastive loss module and model-based intervention planner. Section 5 presents the experimental designs, data sets, base-line models and evaluation metrics. Section 6 presents empirical results, through predictive performance, early-warning capacity, cascade suppression activities. And explores main contributions, managerial implications, and interpretability related issues of the framework. Then we discuss the limitations and opportunities for future work. Lastly, Section 7 concludes the work by summarizing contributions and emphasizing that the focus has moved from forecasting to causal control in supply chain resilience. II Literature Review 2.1 Cascading Failures and Systemic Risk in Supply Chains Global supply chains are characterized by high levels of interdependence, which naturally render them susceptible to cascading failures, in which isolated perturbations spread throughout layers and geographies. Early system-oriented investigations inform the ways in which national contingencies such as pandemics, climate catastrophes, cyber attacks, and geopolitical spats can turn multiple supply chain layers fragile to congested bottlenecks and extreme shortages (Khan et al., 2022) [1]. These systemic risks have been accentuated by the growing use of outsourcing and lean operating practices that improve efficiency at the cost of resilience. Yang et al. (2021) [2] quantitatively investigated this issue by constructing a model of underload-driven cascading failures and showed that demand shocks can induce out-of-proportion system collapse despite mechanisms including safety stock and backup suppliers. Subsequent to this, network cascading failure models have been used for large-scale physical and trade networks. Xu et al. (2024) [3] studied the impact of port-level disruptions within the Global Container Shipping Network and demonstrated that single-node failures could lead to traffic redistribution and overload across maritime logistics networks. Cascading

segments.text: behavior has also been found in domains other than logis tics, such as in resource and waste market systems. Li et al. (2021)[5] studied the disruption in the global plastic waste trade and showed that capacity overloads spread across international trade networks if reactions are not coordinated. These works taken together support the finding that cascading failures are highly nonlocal, nonlinear and network-structure dependent—and yet we still rely on static models, using but not learning from networks. 2.2 Ripple Effect Analysis and Recovery-Focused Strategies Related studies have investigated the ripple effect by simulating propagation of disruptions in multi-echelon supply chains and analysing post-disruption recovery strategies. KEk et al. [4] employed discrete-event simulation for the analysis of disruption propagation in the copper sector and reported limited sourcing flexibility and lack of adequate safety stock as dominant amplification factors. Manupati et al. Further analyzed recovery strategies in complex supply chain networks and employed blockchain-enabled smart contracts and genetic-algorithm optimization to examine pre- and post-disruption decision-making (2022) [6]. Although these methods can offer significant managerial guidelines, they mainly aim at optimizing responses after disasters break out but not predicting or controlling cascade onset in the early stage. Organizational and managerial aspects Park and Singh (2023) [7] stressed the significance of risk alert tools using big data analytics impact, as they demonstrated empirically that strong IT and analytical capabilities are correlated positively with firms’ capacity to anticipate risks. However, these alert tools usually function as early-warning systems and do not explicitly simulate how risks spread through a supply network in an interdependent manner. Moreover, other reviews on resilience in various domains such as automotive, pharmaceuticals, shipping, semiconductor suggest the importance of proactive adaptive mitigation strategies though they do not provide a comprehensive causal-dynamic prediction framework (Maheshwari & Jaggi, 2024 [10] ), Xiong et al., 2025 [11]). 2.3 Data-Driven Risk Prediction and Digital Supply Chain Surveillance Given the rapid increase in heterogeneous digital data types, machine learning and artificial intelligence have recently been playing significant roles in supply chain risk analytics. Brintrup et al. (2024) [12] proposed the idea of Digital Supply Chain Surveillance, use AI to uncover hidden dependencies and increase visibility across an opaque supply networks. Related work has utilized the event-driven IoT data and deep learning in order to predict logistics failure during natural hazards, with high prediction accuracies but dominated by black-box sequence models (Alzahrani & Asghar, 2023 [13]). Fraud detection is another area where ML has been considered useful in detecting unusual transactions, or operational quirks (though predominantly correlated detection rather than causally for intervention planning) (Lokanan & Maddhesia, 2025 [8]). Finally, system-level modelling methods have also been proposed for the evaluation of infrastructure-supply chain interdependencies. Oliver et al. (2022) [15] integrated model-based systems engineering (MBSE) with discrete-event simulation to assess
segments.label: human

segments.text: infrastructure disruptions impact on critical supply chains. By contrast, in the context of power [Salehpour et al., 2022] and smart grid networks [Ghasemi et al., 2023], similar cascading failure analyses show that considering heterogeneous role composition and component dependencies results in better prediction performance. Although refined methodologies have been developed, these frameworks are still domain specific and do not include learning of generalizable mechanisms to evolve acausal structure. 2.4 Graph Neural Networks and Network-Aware Prediction Models Graph learning is such a powerful paradigm for capturing inter-firm dependencies and spread of disruption. Yang et al. (2024) [18] utilized graph-based models and showed that inter-firm relations enhance the predictive value for post-hazard firm-level sales changes, compared to non-network-based baselines. Further extending GNNs with neurosymbolic reasoning Kosasih and Brintrup (2022) [19] (GNNR), discoveries of hidden supply chain relationships that improve structural visibility can be made. These approaches validate the benefit of relational learning, but are mainly for a purely static or discretetime analysis, without taking into account the causal dynamics. Recent research is becoming more aware that predictive accuracy alone suffices neither for risk prevention. Wyrembek et al. (2025) [17] stated that causal machine learning is key to intervention planning, where decision-makers can reason over “what if” situations corresponding to alternative managerial interventions. But existing methods relying on the causal GNNs often utilize static or slowly evolving causal graphs, are applicable only to acyclic relations, and treat counterfactual analysis as a post process rather than integrated with dynamic decision making. 2.5 Research Gap and Motivation Throughout the literature, three drawbacks remain. To begin with, existing cascading failure research is based on static simulation models that are incapable of prediction and adaptation. Furthermore, the machine learning and GNN-based methods we study mainly cover correlations or static network effects, making it difficult to model time-varying causality and feedback loops. Third, despite its potential, causal and counterfactual design is still not real-time assisted intervention optimization at risk prediction tasks, making it impractical for proactive cascades suppression. This motivates the design of a causality-driven learning framework for continuous-time setting, which can simultaneously predict disruption propagation and optimize mitigation actions together, where this is the basis of our proposed CT-SCaLE model. III Problem Formulation To do this, we define a global supply-chain network infusing dynamics and causality into it as a dynamical system evolving continuously with time. The aim is to forecast the initiation and spread of cascading disruptions [14], as well as to recommend the best interventions to minimize their consequences given resources and budget limitations.

In real supply chains, disruptions propagate asynchronously and their effects accumulate and interact on the short timescales that are typically overlooked by discrete-time models [27]. The dataset is under the form of a multi-level supply chain network extracted from a big fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) firm: the nodes represent operational entities like factories, processing units and distribution centers, and directed arcs model material flow between them or operational conditions. In the present work, we draw samples from a connected subgraph of the network consisting of 1,842 nodes and 4,976 directed edges that was chosen in order to capture realistic multi-echelon interactions yet to keep continuous-time simulation computationally feasible. Each node is characterized by 12 time-dependent features, such as sales activities,

segments.text: production volumes and operational stress markers, obtained at daily resolution. Such temporal node attributes make the data-set suitable to model the evolutions of disruptions and cascading failures in time. We followed a temporal split approach to achieve fair evaluation and avoid data leakage. The timeline, the first 70% of which is used for training, the next 15% for validation and the remainder for testing. This experiment corresponds to a realistic setting in which models need to forecast future disturbances with only available historical data. We choose SupplyGraph as it incorporates both industrial realism and explicit network structure, as well as temporal node dynamics, which provides a more appropriate benchmark for comparing different approaches that pertain to the learning of optimal times in continuous-time causal learning and intervention planning in supply chains. 5.2 Baseline Models Against four representative baseline models that encapsulate distinct modeling assumptions prevailing in supply chain analytics, CT-SCaLE is contrasted as follows: ●​ Static GNN- A message-passing graph neural network that does not evolve over time, i.e., no temporal dynamics in the supply chain graph. Node embeddings are learned by aggregating neighborhoods and predictions are made through feed-forward layers. ●​ Temporal GNN- The network is a temporal graph neural network based learning model with recurrence state update to represent the evolution at each discrete time. Though it accounts for temporal behavior, causal relations are considered as fixed over time. ●​ Causal GNN- A causal graph neural network enforcing a directed acyclic structure and employing counterfactual reasoning in discrete time. Interventions are evaluated post hoc and are not embedded into the optimization loop. ●​ Non-Causal ODE Model- A continuous-time Neural ODE architecture modeling node state evolution without explicit causal structure learning, isolating the benefit of causal reasoning from continuous-time dynamics. All baselines are implemented with comparable parameter budgets and trained under identical optimization settings to ensure fair comparison. 5.3 Evaluation Metrics Model performance is assessed using four complementary metrics that evaluate predictive accuracy, early-warning capability, and mitigation effectiveness. CT-SCaLE, in contrast, exhibits a prompt initial descent of the cascade intensity that stabilizes much before all other models. This rapid contemporaneous convergence provides a basis for the conception of CT-SCaLE as an RTCE that can more rapidly identify, and suppress, those destructive pathways. CT-SCaLE reaches a final plateau level indicating cascade size reduction by 31.4% under optimal intervention strategies as compared to baseline models. The results demonstrate CT-SCaLE’s capability in reducing cascading failures with faster and more robust convergence behavior. 6.7 Discussion We find that our modeling of the supply chain disruption with continuous-time causal dynamics is remarkably superior to the traditional discrete and correlation-based approaches. By learning how causal influence changes at fine scale in time, CT-SCaLE traces high-risk propagation paths earlier and allows interventions on such paths at the right instant. For operators, this entails increasing the actionable early-warning signals for their operations to react faster and choose more cost-efficient mitigation resource allocation over multi-tiered networks. The framework’s learned causal structure and counterfactual simulations offer clear explanations of why disruptions propagate, as opposed to the lack of interpretability in black-box predictive systems, and how targeted actions change outcomes, enabling evidence-based decision making. Significantly, CT-SCaLE is designed for deployment realism: it accounts for partial visibility, asynchronous updates and heterogeneous data feeds, such as those found in a global supply-chain context; and hence can be integrated within enterprise risk dashboards and real-time monitoring systems. Overall, these capabilities establish CTC as a pragmatic and strategically important avenue for the resilient operation of supply chains.

segments.text: 6.8 Limitations and Future Work While CT-SCaLE show promising predictive and intervention performances, it may suffer from the issue of data sparsity in multi-tier supply chains since incomplete visibility restricts the accuracy of learned causal relationships. Furthermore, causal identifiability in continuous-time still remains a challenge under strong confounding and when the external conditions are changing rapidly, highlighting the necessity of richer multimodal integration. In the future, we will further improve the real-time deployment efficiency and other time dimension indices, such as adaptive updating, streaming inference and scalable causal structure learning in order to monitor massive dynamic global networks continuously. VII Conclusion In this paper, we presented CT-SCaLE, a causal learning framework in continuous time that incorporates prediction, explanation and intervention planning for how to counter cascading failures in global supply chains. In contrast to the discrete and correlation-based models, in CT-SCaLE changes in causal influence over time and rapid spread of disruption may be captured, allowing better risk management. Experiments makes a 14.7% improvement in the prediction accuracy, increase the lead time of early warning by 22%, and decreases the size of cascade spread by 31.4% comparing to advanced baselines. Combining causal rationale with real-time intervention optimization, CT-SCALE is steering Supply Chain Analytics away from the bands of forecast toward an actioned, control-oriented resilience. In the future, tests will be conducted aimed at enhancing causal identifiability in sparse data, multimodal integration and real time deployment for large industrial scale networks. ​ References [1] Khan, R.
